Alan Saghatelian, PhD: The Saghatelian Lab studies peptides and metabolites — small molecules in the body whose levels shift during disease, the way low insulin causes diabetes or high cholesterol causes heart disease. Because thousands of these molecules exist, the lab uses mass spectrometry, a technology that measures many small molecules in a single sample, to compare healthy and diseased tissue and identify which molecules are disease-linked. This approach led to discovery of a new human lipid that reduces inflammation and reverses diabetes symptoms in mice, and to a previously unknown cluster of human genes producing peptides involved in DNA repair, relevant to cancer. The lab collaborates broadly to study these molecules' roles in cancer, neurodegenerative disease, and immune disorders, aiming to turn such discoveries into new medicines.
Ali Torkamani, PhD: The Torkamani Lab uses genomics and computational tools — including machine learning and deep learning — to figure out the genetic causes of human disease and predict individual health risks. The lab analyzes genetic markers together with data from wearable sensors to build models that forecast a person's risk of conditions like coronary artery disease and pre-diabetes, and it develops app-based digital tools that turn this genetic and physiological data into personalized risk predictions. These models are being tested in remote clinical trials that pair a person's predicted risk with tailored behavioral and therapeutic interventions. The lab also works on interpreting whole genomes to discover rare disease genes and to communicate genetic risk information to patients, aiming to move from broad population statistics to individualized predictions that restore people to their personal health baseline.
Dennis Burton, PhD: The Burton Lab studies broadly neutralizing antibodies — rare antibodies that can block infection by many different strains of a fast-mutating virus, unlike typical antibodies that work against only one strain. The lab pioneered methods for isolating and characterizing these antibodies against HIV, and more recently against coronaviruses, and has shown they can protect against infection in animal models. By studying how these antibodies physically latch onto viral surface proteins (including how they use lipids to recognize HIV), the lab identifies the precise viral targets vaccines should aim at. This structural and molecular work feeds directly into vaccine design, with candidate molecules being tested in animal models and moving toward the clinic. The research is carried out through large NIH- and Gates Foundation-funded consortia aimed at developing an HIV vaccine and defending against other viral threats.
Bryan Briney, PhD: The Briney Lab studies antibodies and vaccine design against difficult, fast-evolving viruses, including HIV, Lassa, SARS-related coronaviruses, influenza, dengue, malaria, and hepatitis C. The lab works on stimulating the rare, hard-to-elicit antibodies needed to broadly fight HIV, and has identified new antibodies and vaccine targets by comparing protein structures across different lineages of the Lassa virus. The team has also discovered antibodies that provide broad immunity against SARS-related coronaviruses, including emerging variants, and is developing approaches that target young immune cells as a strategy for building vaccines against multiple pathogens. With NIH and other funding, the lab works to uncover how viruses like those causing COVID-19, Lassa, and Ebola evolve, information that supports designing vaccines and therapeutic antibodies that could be stockpiled ahead of future pandemics.
Sergio Catz, PhD: The Catz Lab studies vesicular transport — how cells package and move molecules internally and to their surface, a process essential to nearly all cell functions, including immune responses. The lab focuses on processes like autophagy, cytokine secretion, phagocytosis, and formation of neutrophil extracellular traps, and on the Rab proteins that organize these trafficking pathways. Using super-resolution microscopy, functional assays, animal models, and cell systems, the lab maps how these mechanisms work and go wrong in diseases such as coronary artery disease, lysosomal storage disorders, and autoimmune conditions like lupus. The lab has also built high-throughput screening methods to find small molecules that block or activate vesicular trafficking, some of which are being tested in preclinical models of these diseases, with the goal of turning this basic cell biology into new therapeutic strategies.
Michael Boddy, PhD: The Boddy Lab studies how cells detect and repair DNA damage, and what happens when this repair machinery fails — a breakdown linked to cancer and premature aging. The lab combines cell biology, proteomics, genetics, and protein structural biology to dissect these repair pathways. It discovered a new family of proteins called STUbLs that link two cellular tagging systems (SUMO and ubiquitin), revealing how cells respond to DNA damage and how a leukemia drug works. The lab also found that a DNA repair protein can mimic SUMO's structure to hijack the SUMO pathway rather than simply being modified by it, raising the possibility that other proteins use similar tricks to control this system. The lab additionally studies how these same DNA repair factors help cells detect and respond to viral and gene-therapy DNA, connecting DNA repair biology to antiviral immunity.
Mansun Law, PhD: The Law Laboratory's mission is to generate foundational insights in virology and immunology that could help eradicate hepatitis B (HBV) and hepatitis C (HCV) — two viral infections that cause chronic liver disease worldwide. The lab applies a wide range of technologies to study viral hepatitis, how chronic infections persist, antibody responses, B cells (the immune cells that make antibodies), and vaccine design. In one line of work, the lab tested vaccine-like particles that mimic the appearance of the virus and found they triggered a stronger antibody response in mice than immunizing with hepatitis C proteins alone, a finding relevant to designing more effective vaccines. Overall, the lab works to understand how the immune system can be trained to recognize and clear these hard-to-treat chronic viral infections.
